posts.author: jack wang
posts.text: @ForecastQuant This is why the power law fits keep loosening — time was never the driver, it was just riding on adoption, hashrate and liquidity all compounding together. Once ETF flows decouple from on-chain adoption, the proxy breaks and the curve bends. Describes, doesn't explain, exactly.
posts.reply_en: 👀 Exactly: time is the proxy, adoption is the engine. If ETF flows keep decoupling from on-chain activity, what breaks first in your view: the power-law floor or the upper band?
posts.visual: gráfico: precio BTC en escala log-log vs ajuste power law con bandas, marcando el inicio de los ETF spot (ene 2024); fondo azul marino, Bitcoin en blanco, acentos lima, logo como marca de agua

posts.author: Mestray
posts.text: @Khaikhaidao @ForecastQuant @era_wallet The silent part is that the old address keeps looking fine while new funds land on a different path. I write the derivation path next to the seed backup, so a restore test shows any change.
posts.reply_en: 👀 Writing the path next to the seed is underrated: m/84' and m/44' give two completely different address sets from the same 24 words. Do you also note the first receive address to check on restore?

posts.author: Mestray
posts.text: @Khaikhaidao @ForecastQuant @era_wallet Most wallet update flows never show the derivation path at all, so nothing looks wrong until funds land in an address you never backed up. Re-derive once from your own seed and compare the full address before funding.
posts.reply_en: ⚠️ That's the scary failure mode: same seed, different path, and the backup looks fine until you restore. I check the first address on an airgapped device before funding anything. I wrote about airgapped self-custody: https://x.com/forecastquant/status/2116083014815924397
